notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 1 of your 5k PB Training Plan

Congratulations on entering a 5km event. Here is some information to help you decide which level of the plan will make you the fittest, fastest and strongest on race day.

We have three different volume/difficulty levels of our 5k PB Training Plan. They are a reflection on how much time you have available to train, and how much running experience you have, rather than a reflection on your goal time for the event. Some runners will be able to complete 5km in < 25 mins following the intermediate plan, and other runners might take >30 mins following the advanced plan.

You need to choose a level that you feel will be sustainable for the entire 8-week program. Your body needs to be able to comfortably cope with the volume without causing you illness or injuries, and your training schedule needs to be able to fit around all of the other aspects of your day-to-day life, such as work and family commitments.

You don’t have to stick to the same level for the entire plan (you have access to all three levels), you can go up or down levels depending on your time availability and how your body is coping with the volume. The key is consistency. You need to choose the level that allows you to run every week without needing any enforced rest.

Read the description in the Glossary Tab to decide whether you should follow the beginner, intermediate or advanced plan.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
Running Technique

You need to start by working on the absolute foundation of what will lead to a successful race. Your running technique. It doesn’t matter how many stretches or exercises you do, if your running technique is not up to scratch, you will be much more likely to suffer a number of common running injuries and you will never reach your full potential.

Watch this video to learn how to run with good technique.

Strength Vs Stability

To be able to run and avoid injuries, you need to have good hip and pelvis stability. When working properly, the role of the stability muscles is to stabilise your skeleton and spine in the optimal position so the bigger, stronger muscles can develop force and create movement.

The ability to stand on one foot with your eyes closed for 60 seconds requires you to have good stability – We are going to test this in a minute .

I have often seen clients who can squat 100kg, or perform 100 sit-ups, but if they can’t stand on one foot for a minute, then the relative strength of their “movement” muscles is not going to help their running performance.

Test Your Stability Now

To get an understanding of stability, I want you to do this simple one minute test. Stand on one leg, close your eyes. Start counting in seconds 1, 2, 3…………

How long did you last until you had to put your foot down?.

If you made it to

- less than 10… You have a lot of work to do

- 10 – 30 ……. Still not good. Your lack of hip stability might cause some injuries

- 30 – 45 …….. Better, but still room for improvement

- 60 seconds …….. Great. Keep doing what you are doing

Record your results because we are going to test this again later in the plan

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
We have put together an awesome weekly guide on how to manage your food and hydration during training and for race day. Nailing your nutrition is equally as important as following the training and recovery sessions, so I urge you to follow this advice.

This week, the focus is on “Just Eat Real Food”

Following the “JERF” principle is an excellent way to guide your meal and snack choices – it is also referred to as a “whole foods” diet.

This is food that comes out of the ground, off a tree or from an animal – and that has been processed minimally – if at all.

This will provide you with a very nutrient dense diet and will make a significant impact on your overall health and wellbeing. Not only due to the nutrients that you are putting in, but also due to what you are leaving out. Packaged foods most often contain highly refined vegetables oils, chemicals, flavour enhancers, preservatives and refined sugars – which all play havoc with your liver, metabolism and hormones.

The foods you choose provide the body with the building blocks and nutrients it requires for cell growth and DNA replication – this has a direct impact on your muscles, ligaments, immune system and vitality. Quality of food is as important as the quality of training and rest – these 3 combined is what influences your performance and recovery.

…. “you are what you eat”

Your homework this week.

The single biggest thing you can do to improve your nutrition is meal planning. If you have good food ready and available in the fridge you are 90% there.

Being organised and planning ahead is critical – shopping, preparing and some cooking. Allocate a couple of hours on the weekend or one evening to write down the next few days meals, and then shop accordingly – online and delivery services make this even easier

Jot down your meals for the week and see if you can make some healthy improvements to your diet.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 2 of your 5k PB Training Plan

I hope you enjoyed your first week on the training plan. The first week included an overview into how to improve your running technique, some exercises to improve your core stability and we also introduced the 3 minute morning ritual.

Start making great running habits now. Stick to the body maintenance in the plan. It really will make you stronger, help you to avoid injury, and ensure you enjoy your 5km event.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
Running Technique

Have you started to focus on your running technique yet? The sooner you learn to run with good technique the better. It is a VITAL component in the quest to staying injury free, and running faster.

In the video I refer to the importance of “cadence”. Cadence is the number of steps per minute you take when you are running. Running with the correct cadence is integral to good running form, and therefore also integral to staying injury-free. We will talk more about this as the weeks progress.

Uphill Running Technique

“Rolling Hills” feature a lot in this program, so now is the perfect time to learn how to run uphills efficiently.

Rolling hills is the term we use to describe running over a course that is consistently going up and downhill for the duration of your run. Plan ahead and identify a course that has a good amount of up and downhill. The hills don’t have to be steep but they should be as regular as possible throughout the course. Consider running a short hilly loop multiple times if you don’t have access to a long hilly route. You should average approximately 150m – 250m of vertical elevation per 10km of running on rolling hills.

The better your form when you run up the hills the faster you will be and the more energy you will conserve for later in the race.

Watch this video to learn what to focus on every time you are running uphill.

Accelerations

This week we are adding accelerations to the program. Accelerations are 20 to 40 second efforts building from an easy jog to a relaxed hard effort, and then easing back down to a jog again. Focus on running tall and keeping your cadence high and your strides short. Slowly walk or jog for 1 minute between accelerations. The purpose of accelerations is improve your leg speed, hip mobility, glute strength and your running technique. NB: They are not a sprinting or speed work session.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
Do you stick to a weekly food plan? Planning your food in advance will certainly help you make better food choices. Nutrition is a critical part of your training and helps your body recover and get stronger.

This week we are covering the important role of carbohydrates in your training.

Carbohydrates are your body’s preferred source of energy. They are the backbone of an endurance athlete’s diet.

Your body turns carbohydrates into glucose (energy). The brain requires a significant amount of glucose (or energy) to operate efficiently, maintain concentration, avoid mood swings and avoid sugar cravings.

Intake needs to be adjusted depending on expected energy output / activity level – as only a finite amount of carbohydrates can be used as fuel or stored as glycogen, with any left over carbohydrate potentially being stored as fat.

Excess carbohydrates can cause the body to make too much insulin leading to high blood sugar levels and then rapid decreases – or fluctuating energy levels ( 3pm slump anyone? ). This happens more often when simple, processed carbohydrates are being consumed instead of complex carbohydrates.

So what should you eat and how much is enough?

Most people following an ultra marathon training program will need between 3-6 grams of carbs per kilo of body weight per day.

For example a 70kg athlete may have anywhere from 210gms carbs per day to 420gms per day – it is a large variation… as it depends on body type and exercise load.

The majority of carbs should be whole unrefined complex carbohydrates ie vegetables, fruit and whole grains.

However, not all are created equal – so it is important to understand the carbohydrate load of different fruit, vegetables and grains.

For example – starchy carbs are much higher in carbohydrate load – this includes vegetables that grow below the ground like potato and sweet potato, also grains such as oats, corn, rice, quinoa, and legumes, beans and peas.

If your goal is to reduce your weight then it is best to avoid too many of these starchy carbs – or only have them as part of your post training meal. I will cover this in detail in the coming weeks.

This week, I want you to stick with following your JERF ( just eat real food) plan from last week. Try and make it more of a habit

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 3 of your 5k PB Training Plan

“Inappropriate speedwork sessions cause more injuries than any other type of running training”

But – that doesn’t mean you shouldn’t do any.

It just means you need to be careful and introduce it gradually. This week we will be adding some fartleks to your training program. The goal is to build your strength and speed safely each week, not to go out and break yourself!

Speedwork is included in almost every training plan, for every race, I have ever seen.

All of the world’s elite athletes do some sort of speed sessions in their training, therefore it has been adopted by coaches across the world and used to train athletes of all abilities.

The problem with this is that not many of us have bodies which function like elite athletes and in our haste to get better, we push beyond our ability.

I don’t just mean raw talent or speed, I actually mean that we don’t have the ankle flexibility, the hip mobility or the power-to-weight ratio that elite athletes have.

They spend their lives training, eating and sleeping. We spend our lives sitting at desks, sitting on sofas, looking after kids, stuck in traffic and squeezing in training where we can. Our modern lifestyles compromise our body’s ability to tolerate speedwork, therefore it has to be integrated very carefully into a training program.

This week we are adding Fartleks

Fartlek workouts are interval training sessions where you alternate moderate-to-hard efforts with easy aerobic running. The Fartlek intervals should be done in the middle of the day’s total mileage, so there should be some easy running before and after the intervals to warm up and cool down.

For example, “7km with 6 * 1 min Fartlek @ tempo pace, 2 min recovery jog” means the total run is 7km. You might warm up for 2km then run for 1 minute at tempo pace, then jog for 2 minutes to recover and repeat this 6 times. Then finish the run at an aerobic pace to make up the 7km total distance.

(Note: Fartleks are not in the beginner program this week)

Park Run and Tempo Run

A local park run is a great way to practise the tempo run as part of your training plan. At tempo pace, you should be able to talk while running in short sentences or a few words at a time. These sessions are great training for your 10km race.

Go to www.parkrun.com.au to learn more about Park Runs. You can replace a park run with a 5km run on the flat or small rolling hills if there isn’t a convenient park run near you.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
When we run fast, there are a few things that happen to our body:

- There is more ground reaction force exerted on our bodies – i.e. more pressure on our muscles, tendons and joints.

- Our stride lengthens – this requires more flexibility through the hip joint, ankle joint, calf muscles, achilles tendon, quadriceps muscles and hip flexors. NB: If you run with good form your stride length should increase behind your body, not in front of it.

- NB: If you run with good form your stride length should increase behind your body, not in front of it.

- Potential to “Overstride” – As we speed up we risk over-striding, which further increases the ground reaction forces we subject our body to. NB: “Overstride” refers to increasing your stride length in front of your body, which is poor technique.

- NB: “Overstride” refers to increasing your stride length in front of your body, which is poor technique.

- Our cadence often increases – which along with increased stride length and speed, puts more stress on our heart and lungs.

- Our running technique can suffer – due to a lack of strength, flexibility and stability. The faster the pace, the worse our technique usually becomes.

- We fatigue quickly during speed sessions which reduces our ability to absorb load and can lead to injury.

Because of these changes in stress and form which occur when we run fast, and because our modern day lifestyles inhibit the way our body’s function, inappropriate speedwork sessions cause more injuries than any other type of running training.

There are three possible ways to increase your speed when you run:

- Increase your stride length

- Increase you cadence

- A combination of both

Ideally your cadence needs to stay between 175 – 185 steps/minute in order to remain efficient. Lower than 175 and you don’t use the elastic recoil of your calf muscle and achilles tendon efficiently. Higher than 185 and you will elevate your heart rate higher than necessary which leads to early fatigue.

Therefore, in order to run faster properly, it only leave us with the option of increasing our stride length. BUT – your stride needs to lengthen behind you, not in front of you. You still need your foot to land close to under your body in order to run efficiently and to stay injury free.

Watch the video below on how to run faster and practice the drill included in this video.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
An ongoing issue that athletes face is maintaining a strong immune system – especially when you are in a peak training phase. You need to make sure you are providing your body with the correct nutrition and resources to protect yourself from colds, flu’s and viruses.

You need to be aiming for a minimum of 5 serves of vegetables and 1-2 serves of fruit per day.

Not only do you need the carbohydrate that they offer, but also the nutrient density. If you are struggling to include enough – smoothies are a great way to boost you intake. You could use fruit, vegetables, add in some matcha tea powder (high in anti-oxidants) plus a handful of nuts or seeds.

Getting adequate sleep is also an extremely important part of protecting your immune system. This is often overlooked when training for a specific event, especially when the training load increases – as extra training hours are often prioritised over sleep – this is NOT a good strategy and often ends up compromising the immune system or contributing to fatigue. Most athletes need 7-8 hours sleep per night.

Your homework this week – Eat 5 serves of vegetables and 1-2 serves of fruit per day

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 4 of your 5k PB Training Plan

Good news. This week is a recovery week in the 8 week program, so the long run is shorter and the Thursday session is easier.

By reducing the volume and intensity of the training this week, it will allow your body a chance to recover from the fatigue and tight muscles which will have been building up over the last three weeks. The recovery week will set you up to be fresh and raring to go for the next build phase of the program.

Despite the reduced running volume, this is NOT A REST WEEK .

You need to continue with the same number of runs per week and be just as diligent (if not, more so) with your body maintenance sessions. A week of complete rest will probably leave you feeling tired and sluggish and less motivated to get back into the training next week. The aim of the recovery week is to keep your body and your brain used to running, whilst still logging some all-important km’s in the training diary.

We have focused on running technique for the last three weeks. Make sure you keep it “front of mind” during every run.

Bad habits have a tendency to start creeping in as you become fatigued. Towards the end of the long run is when you are most likely to revert back to over-striding and dropping your cadence.

One strategy to combat this drop in form is to have short walking breaks. You might be one hour into the long run, for example, feeling tired and starting to slump down and overstride.

If you walk for a couple of minutes then start running again, you will be more likely to be able to maintain a good posture and cadence. You can have as many walking breaks as you need to throughout the run as they won’t have a negative effect on your endurance, and they will ultimately increase your chances of being able to stick with this program.

Keep this little mantra running through your head, especially when you are tired “stand up tall, short steps, stand up tall, short steps, stand up tall . . . “

NB: All of the runs this week are at an easy or “aerobic” pace. There is often a temptation to run faster during recovery weeks because the volume is so much lower. DON’T RUN FAST THIS WEEK, if you do, then it won’t actually be recovery.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
Body Maintenance

I have talked a lot about how important stability is for runners. As a reminder watch the below video covering what we are trying to achieve with the stability exercises. The aim and purpose of the exercises is to “teach” your hips and pelvis to be stable when you run. If your hips and pelvis remain stable then your energy is used to drive your body forwards, rather than losing a lot of that energy to bobbing up and down, and twisting and turning.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
Last week, you should have set up an account with My Fitness Pal, or a similar app, to start tracking the amount of protein and carbohydrates you are consuming.

This week we are going to take a look at Healthy Fats – why are they important and where do they come from?

Healthy fats are essential. Healthy fats will NOT make you fat, in fact they will help you to lose weight. Healthy fats help to make you feel full and satisfied, so that you don’t over consume calories. Fat is essential for cell membranes, hormone production and also for transport and absorption of nutrients – especially vitamins A,D,E and K.

Each meal should contain a small amount of fat – this is pretty easy when you are following the “JERF” principle and hitting your protein requirement – as fat is often “packaged” with protein – as you will see from the list below.

An easy way to increase fat in your diet is to drizzle a small amount of olive oil on your vegetables and salads.

Another popular way for athletes to increase fat intake is to consume MCT oil in a coffee (it’s called “bulletproof” coffee). MCT (Medium Chain Triglyceride) is from coconut oil, and is an excellent source of healthy fat.

The human body can make most of the types of fats it needs from other fats or raw materials. However, that is not the case for omega-3 fatty acids – the body can’t make them from scratch, but must get them from food. They are therefore called Essential Fatty Acids. One of the easiest, most convenient and economical ways to increase your Omega 3 intake is to eat tinned Sardines.

A lot of people are happy to eat tinned Tuna, which provides around 150mg of Omega 3 per serve, but Sardines provide 2900mg per serve – nearly 20 times as much.

There is no set standard for how much combined EPA/DHA you need each day, although healthy experts generally recommend 250mg – 500mg per day. So one tin of tuna per day is not enough, whereas if you had tinned Sardines 2 times per week instead –you are smashing it.

Before screw up our nose and say “yuck” …. Spend the $3 and just try them …you might be surprised.

My favourite way is to have them as part of a big salad for lunch, others enjoy them on sourdough toast, or just straight from the tin as a snack.

Examples of healthy fats

- Oils – Coconut Oil, Olive Oil, Flaxseed Oil, Nut Oils

- Animal Fats – skin on chicken, lard, egg yolks

- Fatty Fish – Salmon, Mackerel and Sardines,

- Full Fat Dairy foods – choose good quality butter, yoghurt, ricotta cheese, full fat milk, cheese, haloumi

- All Nuts and Seeds – examples are cashews, brazil, walnuts, sunflower, pepitas, linseeds, chia, hemp

- Fruits – Avocado, Coconut

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 5 of your 5k PB Training Plan

Training Advice

We are now getting into some bigger training weeks.

The combination of longer weekend runs and either a fartlek or hill repeats sessions during the week is putting your body under more stress. If you are consistent with the stretches and exercises, and you are following the running plan so that there are not any big jumps in volume, then your body should tolerate the increased load and you will become stronger and faster.

If you have a few niggles starting to appear that you are worried about, here are some strategies you should use to help keep them under control.

Adopt the “little and often” philosophy . Breaking your weekly distance into shorter but more regular runs will be easier for your body to cope with.

- In an ideal training program the long run is important, but it is counter-productive if you then have to miss 2-3 days of training because of it.

- For example – you could split the total volume of your long run between Saturday and Sunday, or Sunday and Monday – so that your overall weekly volume remains similar, but you don’t have the extra stress of a really long run for your body to cope with.

Speedwork – Don’t do any! Whether it is hill reps or tempo park runs. If you have got a niggle then leave any speed sessions out of your program until the niggle has settled.

- You will get a lot more benefit out of being able to continue to train than you will from persevering with speedwork and potentially making an injury worse.

Self Massage – sit down every evening and massage your sore bits (usually calves, feet, ITBs)

- A foam roller can be helpful for I TBs, quads and calves

- A tennis ball or golf ball can be useful for the sole of your foot (through the arch of your foot – not over the heel or the bony bits near the ball of your foot)

- A trigger point ball can be useful for your glute muscles

Ice – Icing a swollen achilles tendon, an inflamed ITB, or a painful foot can be a great way to help settle your symptoms in time to be able to run again the next day.

- Use ice cubes in a plastic bag NOT one of those blue gel packs. If ice cubes are not possible then frozen peas will (just) suffice. Ice cubes stay at a constant temperature (0 degrees) until they have melted. Ice packs usually start off too cold (-7 degrees) and warm up too quickly, so they can give you a nasty “freezer burn” and they don’t stay cold long enough to be effective.

Stretching – stretching your calf muscles for example can help to reduce the tension in your Achilles tendon. Stretching your glute muscles can help to reduce ITB and knee symptoms.

Most importantly – “Listen to your Body” – if you are concerned about a niggle or an injury during your training, then get it diagnosed by a trusted health care professional and take some proactive steps towards managing it and getting treatment if required.

Do not try and stick to the weekly km if you do have an issue. Continuing to push through pain when you have a problem could stop you turning up on race day.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
This week we are going to focus on hill repeats and accelerations as part of our mid week runs.

Hill repeats are repeated short segments of harder uphill running. They increase aerobic power, high-intensity fatigue resistance, pain tolerance, and run-specific strength. The ideal hill on which to run hill repeats is a steady, moderate gradient of 4 to 6 percent and about 250m long.

NB: During hill repeats you should be breathing hard and only able to speak 2 or 3 words at a time. BUT YOU ARE NOT SPRINTING!

Accelerations are 20 to 40 second efforts building from an easy jog to a relaxed hard effort, and then easing back down to a jog again. Focus on running tall and keeping your cadence high and your strides short. Slowly walk or jog for 1 minute between accelerations.

The purpose of accelerations is improve your leg speed and your stride mechanics. Keep in mind that they are meant to be fun, and something to look forward to after an easy run. They are NOT a sprinting session.

Don’t forget the running technique mantra we started last week “stand up tall, short steps, stand up tall, short steps, stand up tall . . . “

Even if you feel like you have “mastered” your technique, watch this video again. It is amazing the little extra things you can pick up that you may have missed the first time around.

Cadence

In the running technique video I refer to the importance of running with the correct cadence. Cadence is the number of steps per minute you take. There is a bit of controversy around whether there is a specific number you should aim for. The “golden number” of 180 – is often quoted.

I am a huge believer that 180 is the gold standard and something that you should all ultimately be aiming for.

What should you do to improve your cadence?

The best way to work on improving your cadence is to use a metronome. You can buy a small, clip-on, digital metronome that is perfect for the purpose, or if you run with your phone, you can download a metronome app and use that. Set the metronome to the appropriate beat, and run in time with the beeps (one foot landing each time you hear a beep).

Follow these steps to make sure you do it accurately and safely

- Measure your cadence. During the middle of a normal training run, count your steps on one foot (i.ee just your left) for a minute on a section of flat ground. Double it. This will give you your cadence. Repeat this several times over several runs to work out an accurate average.

- It is difficult to increase your cadence by more than 10 steps/minute in any one go. If your cadence is 160, for example, you should set your metronome to 170 and get used to that for a month, before increasing it further to 180.

- Continue using the metronome for as long as you need to until 180 becomes your natural / subconscious gait pattern.

There are two common, but temporary, repercussions of increasing your cadence that you should be aware of.

- It will increase your heart rate. Expect to breathe a bit harder, and get tired a bit quicker than you have been used to. Your cardio-vascular system will adjust over time, but expect it to take 2-3 months to fully adjust.

- Your calf muscles will probably do more work, and get tighter. As our stride gets shorter, our foot usually lands flatter, which uses the calf muscle more. Your calf muscles will get stronger with time, but some extra stretching and/or foam rolling will help during the transition.

I have been working as a physiotherapist treating running injuries for nearly 30 years, and I have spent the last 15 years working with thousands of runners to improve their technique and reduce their injuries.

Cadence has been one of the most effective and beneficial changes most of those runners have made .

If you want to take your running to the next level, and you haven’t yet focused on your cadence, make sure you do. It can transform your running.

If you like running with music, it is possible to use an app to play music at a certain number of beats per minute. It is much harder though, to follow the rhythm of music than it is to follow the simple beat of a metronome, so I would highly recommend using a simple metronome app initially, and once you have become accustomed to the higher cadence and it feels natural, then you could switch back to running with music.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
An ongoing issue that athletes face is maintaining a strong immune system – especially when you are in a peak training phase. You need to make sure you are providing your body with the correct nutrition and resources to protect yourself from colds, flu’s and viruses.

Endurance running compromises the immune system as oxidative stress is increased; it is important to counter this with an increase in Anti Oxidant foods to counter the free radicals and restore balance. Reducing oxidative stress is also critical as it helps to protect damage to the mitochondria – the powerhouse of our energy production.

Key Anti Oxidant Nutrients:

Vitamin C, Vitamin E, Vitamin A and Co Q10

Antioxidant food sources:

- Capsicum, Broccoli, Dark Green Leafy Veg, Tomatoes, Sweet Potato

- Berries and Citrus Fruits, Papaya, Kiwi

- Green Tea and Matcha Tea

- Organ meats – Liver, heart

- Oily Fish – sardines, mackerel and salmon

- Nuts and Seeds

How many of these foods do you include on a daily basis?

You need to be aiming for a minimum of 5 serves of vegetables and 1-2 serves of fruit per day. Not only do you need the carbohydrate that they offer, but also the nutrient density. If you are struggling to include enough – smoothies are a great way to boost you intake. You could use fruit, vegetables, add in some matcha tea (powder) plus a handful of nuts or seeds.

If you don’t like the sound of organ meats, you can buy some mince meat that has it added, you won’t even know the difference! Or include a good quality pate into your regular diet.

Many athletes benefit from good quality antioxidant supplements, especially if your diet is lacking in these essential nutrients. Seek advice from a qualified nutritionist or naturopath regarding supplements to ensure that your investment is going to be of maximum benefit to you.

This week, I want you to consciously try and include 5 serves of vegetables a day. If you already doing this, then stick to it. If you are not currently eating 5 serves of veges per day then start trying. to improve it, so that your diet is complementing all of your training effort

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 6 of your 5k PB Training Plan

We are increasing volume again this week. It is VITAL, that you “listen to your body” and adjust your training volume and intensity according to how your body is coping. If, for example, you have a niggly knee or a calf muscle which is not coping well with the long run, you could:

- Split the long run into two separate runs For example, run 10km on Sunday and 4km on Monday. Although this is slightly less ideal than completing the long run, it will allow you to maintain the overall weekly volume, and minimise the risk of flaring up your knee or calf muscle injury.

- For example, run 10km on Sunday and 4km on Monday. Although this is slightly less ideal than completing the long run, it will allow you to maintain the overall weekly volume, and minimise the risk of flaring up your knee or calf muscle injury.

- Try Walking / Hiking instead of running We can usually still walk even when running has become uncomfortable or painful. If you think your body might not cope with the long run which is scheduled, then think about opting for the equivalent time walking/hiking instead.

- We can usually still walk even when running has become uncomfortable or painful. If you think your body might not cope with the long run which is scheduled, then think about opting for the equivalent time walking/hiking instead.

This week we are adding a Fartlek session to the intermediate and advanced program. Fartlek workouts are interval training sessions where you alternate moderate-to-hard efforts with easy aerobic running. The Fartlek intervals should be done in the middle of the day’s total mileage, so there should be some easy running before and after the intervals to warm up and cool down.

For example, “8km with 6 * 1 min Fartlek @ tempo pace, 2 min recovery jog” means the total run is 8km. You might warm up for 2km then run for 1 minute at tempo pace, then jog for 2 minutes to recover and repeat this 6 times. Then finish the run at an aerobic pace to make up the 8km total distance.

Please remember: As the volume increases, so does your risk of injury and slipping back into bad running form.

As a reminder, keep this little mantra running through your head, especially when you are tired “stand up tall, short steps, stand up tall, short steps, stand up tall . . . “

Hopefully you followed last week’s advice, to start working on your cadence. If not, check out the info tab on week 5 of your plan.

Don’t just jump straight into running at a cadence of 180 if your body isn’t used to it. You need to measure your current cadence, and increase it by a maximum of 10 steps/minute, allow your body time to adjust to that, and then increase it by another 10 steps/minute if required.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
You should now be eating loads of veggies, have a system to monitor your food intake and be a vision of health! The next thing to think about is what to eat when, to ensure your body is getting exactly what it needs, when it most needs it.

This week we are going to focus on what to eat after training.

Your post training meal is vitally important to stimulate muscle glycogen replacement, protein synthesis and blunting of cortisol (so you don’t end up with Adrenal fatigue). Its needs to be consumed within 45mins post training.

If your session is a tough one – and greater than 60mins, it is vital that you get this meal right in order to get the most from your training and progress with your goals. This meal needs to contain carbohydrates and protein. The carbs refuel the glycogen and blunts cortisol production (both are vital for weight control) and the protein helps repair the muscles and supports the immune system.

The amount that you need to consume for this meal depends on your body weight, the amount of training you are doing, and your personal goals. As a rough guide you should be looking for around 1 gram of carbs per kilo of body weight, and around 1/3 rd of your body weight in protein.

So for example an athlete that weighs 60 kilos, would have 60grams of carbs and 20 grams of protein for this recovery meal. If your session has been an extended session – like a very long run – the need for carbohydrates increases, you might need 1.5-2grams of carbs per kilo of body weight. If the session is 60mins or less, aim for 40gms carb and 10-15 protein.

Choose good quality nutrient dense carbohydrates like fruit, starchy veg, wholegrains, legumes, nuts and seeds, and good quality protein such as eggs, fish, lean meat and dairy. This will ensure that your body is getting the nutrients it needs to have you in the best health possible on race day.

Post training breakfast might be:

- Fruit with Yoghurt, topped with nuts and Seeds or muesli

- Eggs and Toast – can add spinach or Avo

- Smoothie

- Frittata with potato/sweet potato, corn

- Porridge made with milk, topped with fruit, or yoghurt, drizzle honey

Post training dinner might be:

- Chicken Stir fry with Brown rice

- Steak with sweet potato and greens

- Grilled fish with buckwheat, beetroot and spinach salad

- Homemade hamburgers with a large leafy green side salad.

This week stick with all the great work you are doing and start experimenting with your post run meal. If you get a chance, mark down what you eat and note if you feel better the next day, so you start to get an idea of what works for you

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 7 of your 5k PB Training Plan

It is time to start tapering

This week sees a significant reduction in the length of the long run, and a “fairly easy” mid week session. The other runs remain unchanged.

By maintaining both the frequency and intensity of the runs, but dropping the total volume, it will give your legs a chance to recover from the hard training over the past 6 weeks, whilst at the same time keeping them used to ticking over. This tapering effect will also allow your immune system and overall energy levels to improve, which will have you fresh and raring to go on race day.

It is also time to get more sleep!

One of the best ways to help your body recover from the past few weeks of heavy training is to sleep more. Research shows that athletic performance improves with sufficient sleep. Rested athletes are faster.

Get whatever extra sleep you can over the next 2 weeks. 30 minutes here, and 30 minutes there all counts. So sleep when you can.

Mental Training

I think it is important to understand the role your mental stamina plays during a race.

You will probably reach a point in your race where you feel exhausted: your legs are tired, your feet hurt, and you feel like the only way that you’ll make it to the finish line without dying is to either slow down, walk, or maybe even crawl

I think there is a strong case to suggest that training our brains will make us faster. Long training runs and speed workouts help us mentally prepare our brains. They teach us that we can keep going even when tired.

On your next run I recommend thinking about some strategies you can use to keep going when the going gets tough.

Ideas like

- spend 1km thanking a single person that helped you make your race. Then someone else the next 1km and so on.

- sing your favourite song in your head to help stop any negative thoughts creeping in.

- Use the alphabet and starting at the letter A, think of a word about why you love running. For example, atmosphere, bananas, cheering …

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
How to manage your nutrition through your taper?

As you head towards race day your training load is decreasing in volume. This can be a difficult time, and many people experience “taper tantrums”.

Your metabolism with still be working well, and even though you are not burning as many calories in training, you will most likely find that you are still eating the same volume of food. It is vital that you stick with the “JERF” principle at this point as you do not want to compromise your immune system.

Many people feel like they are ‘getting a cold” during taper week – its often just imaginary !! – you have put so much work into getting to this point, it is normal to feel anxious about things that could set you back or impact your performance.

If you are prone to weight gain, this is a good week to watch your carb intake closely, and focus on mostly above the ground vegetables, lean protein and healthy fats. There is no need to carb load for a 10km race. This will only make you feel heavy and slow on race day.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 8. The final week of your 5k PB Training Plan

Congratulations on making it this far through the training program. All of the hard work is done, and this weekend you get to reap the rewards of all of that effort.

How To Warm Up on Race Morning

Warming up effectively on race morning acts as an “on” switch for the brain and body, preparing your muscles to work efficiently during the race.

Try to eat breakfast 2 hours before the race starts if possible, and prepare your race gear the night before the race to help avoid any last minute disasters. Arrive at the start with plenty of time to go to the bathroom and get sorted. I recommend a short 5 min jog with some accelerations 20-minutes before the race starts to help get your body moving. This should also help calm your brain from all the pre-race nerves.

This week’s body maintenance

The focus this week is on maintaining flexibility and mobility to help prevent your joints and muscles stiffening up over the course of this week. The reduction in training, and change in routine, can have a negative impact on your body, so it is very important to keep up with this mobility training.

NB: For any of you following the program who haven’t been doing these stretches and exercises regularly – DON’T START NOW! – Think of it like running training. If you haven’t started your running training yet, then you can’t cram it all into the final week. If you haven’t started stretching or rolling yet, then you definitely shouldn’t try to cram it all into the last week. You will do yourself far more harm than good.

Good Luck – I hope you have a great race

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
Preparing for Race Day

Do you need to carb load this week?

No, for any distance that takes under 3 hours, there is no benefit.

If you do choose to carb load, this does not mean increasing meal size, or calories, but ensuring that each meal does contain predominately carbohydrates, along with a small amount of protein and healthy fat. Vegetables, fruit, legumes and whole grains are excellent sources of carbohydrates.

You may find your weight increases over these few days, as carbohydrates store extra water in your cells – don’t worry, you’ll need the extra water on race day.

Should you drink extra water?

Yes. Hydration levels are critical for athletes, and you should arrive at the race fully hydrated. You should be drinking approximately 2 litres of water a day for 3 days prior to your race, adding a pinch of salt to help increase the uptake of water into the cells. You can also use electrolyte replacement tablets to help increase hydration levels.

Nutrition Guide For Race Day

It is important you know exactly what you are going to eat on race day, and you should have practised this as part of your training. This will put your mind at ease and help you feel prepared.

What should you have for breakfast?

You may feel very nervous on race day morning. Now is NOT the time to consume anything new – (food or fluids) even if it’s free or your friend highly recommends it.

A light breakfast 2 hours prior to the race is ideal – it should be mostly carbohydrates, and around 1-2grams of carb per kilo of body weight.

Eg; if you weigh 60kgs, your breakfast should be 60-120 grams of carbohydrates. If you don’t have much time before the race, stick to the lower end of this scale.

The meal should be low in fibre, low in fat and low in protein, to decrease the risk of gastric upset.

Eg: Banana, White bread, crumpets, honey, fruit juice, sports bar.

30 Grams of carbs :

- 1 medium banana

- 2 slices white bread

- 1.5 crumpets

- 4-6 dates

- 2 Tbs honey

- 1 gel (check label, usually 20-30gms)

- Sports Drink – check label

It is not advisable that you drink sports drink for the hour before the race. Just have your breakfast, and then sip on water. Just prior to the start (i.e. 10-15 mins) you can have a gel if you like.

Fuelling during the race:

By race day you should have practiced a fuelling strategy, and know exactly what your race day nutrition plan is. It is better not to leave it until the night before the race to figure out what you plan to do. For a 10km race you may not require any additional fuel at all during the race. This really depends on how long the race takes you. Over 90 min you may need a gel.

Post Race

If you are still of sound mind in the aftermath of the race, and you want to ensure that you recover from it quickly, you should pay some attention to what you eat in the 45-60 minute period immediately after the race, ideally before you reach for your first beer!

You need to replenish glycogen stores (carbohydrates), plus some protein for muscle recovery. This should be in the ratio 4:1 Carb:Protein. Sports recovery drinks/bars designed for this are great in a race situation as they are very portable. Bananas or chocolate milk are both a great option for straight after your race.

Alcohol is not a good source of hydration. Make sure you hydrate and re-fuel properly before celebrations begin!

glossary.definition:
When you are following the 5k PB Training Plan you will see a number of shorthand descriptions for the different types of running sessions. For example “Hill Reps” or “Fartlek” or “Aerobic Pace”

To use the Training Program properly, and to get the most benefit from it, you need to understand what these session descriptions mean, so that you can use them to best effect in your training.

This beginner-level plan is ideal if you’re relatively new to running — maybe you’ve completed a 5km event or tried a Parkrun, and you’ve done a few short 2–3km runs in recent months. The plan begins with run/walk sessions instead of continuous running, giving your body time to adapt, build strength, and avoid injury as the distances gradually increase.

If you’re brand new to running and haven’t done any consistent training yet, we recommend starting with our Zero to 5K Plan , which is specifically designed for complete beginners.

Beginner runners are aiming to finish the 5km Run, rather than “race” it.

The Intermediate 5K PB Plan kicks off with 23km in the first week and a long run of 5km. It includes structured sessions like fartlek runs, hill repeats, tempo-paced Parkruns, and gradually builds to a 12km long run.

This plan is best suited for runners who’ve been training consistently for at least 6 months and are comfortable running 5–6km regularly. If you haven’t been running regular for the past 6 months, this program may progress too quickly for your body to adapt safely. In that case, we recommend starting with the Beginner Plan to build a stronger foundation and avoid injury.

Intermediate runners are aiming to improve their performance and run a “steady/hard” race.

The Advanced 5K PB Plan starts with 34km in the first week, including an 8km long run. It features structured sessions like fartlek workouts, hill reps, tempo runs, and builds progressively to a 15km long run. This plan is designed to push you — not just to complete 5K, but to race it with intent.

It’s ideal for runners who’ve been training consistently for over a year, are regularly running 10km, and are confident including speed sessions in their weekly routine. If you’re not yet comfortable running 10km or haven’t incorporated speedwork before, the Intermediate or Beginner plans will provide a better foundation.

Advanced runners using this plan are aiming to race hard from start to finish — chasing a personal best with purpose.

This chart shows the long run distance and total weekly volume for each of the three levels. It can help you to choose which level of the plan is the most appropriate one to follow. It will also help you plan your long runs in advance.

Choose the level that suits your current level of fitness. e.g. if you have consistently been running 20-25km per week for the past few months then choose the intermediate level. The advanced plan will ramp up too quickly and potentially cause you an injury. You can always change levels during the plan if you are finding it too easy or too hard.

Accelerations are 20 to 40 second efforts building from an easy jog to a relaxed hard effort, and then easing back down to a jog again. They are to be completed at the end of your run. Focus on running tall and keeping your cadence high and your strides short. Slowly walk or jog for 1 minute between accelerations. The purpose of accelerations is improve your leg speed and your stride mechanics. Keep in mind that they are meant to be fun, and something to look forward to after an easy run. They are NOT a sprinting session.

You should be able to talk comfortably in normal sentences when running at an aerobic pace. The purpose of these sessions is to add more mileage to your week without causing too much fatigue. Aerobic runs improve your running economy to make you a more efficient runner.

A routine of exercises including stretching, stability, strengthening, foam rolling and trigger point ball. The body maintenance routine will be introduced gradually throughout the training program and has been designed to compliment the different phases of the program.

NB: These exercises are an integral part of this training program. The Body Maintenance sessions are equally as important as the running sessions.

Your cross training sessions can be swimming, cycling, pilates, yoga, a low impact gym class, or an easy gym strength session. 30 minutes for aerobic activities like swimming, cycling and gym. 60 minutes for Pilates or Yoga or Stretching Class. These sessions are good for your body as they add to your endurance, but use different muscle groups and are low impact.

Don’t perform a cross training session if you are feeling too fatigued from the current training load.

Fartlek workouts are interval training sessions where you alternate moderate-to-hard efforts with easy aerobic running. The Fartlek intervals should be done in the middle of the day’s total mileage, so there should be some easy running before and after the intervals to warm up and cool down.

For example, “7km with 6 * 1 min Fartlek @tempo pace, 2 min recovery jog” means the total run is 7km. You might warm up for 2km then run for 1 minute at tempo pace, then jog for 2 minutes to recover and repeat this 6 times. Then finish the run at an aerobic pace to make up the 7km total distance.

Pick a flat course for these runs. A few small undulations are ok if you don’t have access to completely flat ground. The purpose of these flat runs is active recovery. They are to help increase your mileage safely, without causing too much fatigue to your system.

Hill repeats are repeated short segments of harder uphill running. They increase aerobic power, high-intensity fatigue resistance, pain tolerance, and run-specific strength. The ideal hill on which to run hill repeats is a steady, moderate gradient of 4 to 6 percent and about 250m long. NB: During hill repeats you should be breathing hard and only able to speak 2 or 3 words at a time. BUT YOU ARE NOT SPRINTING!

The long runs in this plan are designed to be done at an easy, conversational pace — keeping you in your aerobic zone. These runs gradually increase in distance over the course of the plan, helping you build the strength, stamina, and running efficiency needed to finish your 5K feeling strong (and fast). They’re the foundation of your endurance, so keep them relaxed and consistent.
Go to www.parkrun.com.au to learn more about Park Runs. You can replace a park run with a 5km run on the flat or small rolling hills if there isn’t a convenient park run near you.

During the recovery week (Week 4) all of the runs are at aerobic pace and there is significantly less total training volume for the week. We continue with some easy accelerations during the recovery week to help maintain your leg speed and running confidence. The purpose of a recovery week is to let your body and your immune system recover. It will also help to reduce any muscle tightness and niggles. These weeks will help to restore your energy for the next training build phase. Do not do any of these runs fast, and do not run over the stated volumes.

Rest days are vital to help your body recover from the training sessions. Without adequate rest you are more likely to become ill and injured. Try to get as much sleep and recovery time as possible on these days.

Rolling hills is the term we use to describe running over a course that is consistently going up and downhill for the duration of your run. Plan ahead and identify a course that has a good amount of up and downhill. The hills don’t have to be steep but they should be as regular as possible throughout the course. Consider running a short hilly loop multiple times if you don’t have access to a long hilly route. You should average approximately 200m – 250m of vertical elevation per hour of running on rolling hills.

The purpose of this session is to build strength and muscular endurance.

This is the same effort level as “Tempo Pace” below – but your pace will be slower due to it being a hill repeats session. Focus on the level of effort rather than the actual pace you are running. You should be able to talk while running at tempo pace in short sentences or a few words at a time.

Tempo pace should feel comfortably hard — a pace you can sustain, but not one you’d want to hold a conversation at. You might be able to speak in short phrases or a few words at a time, but full sentences will be tough.

As a guide, aim for a pace somewhere between your 10K and half marathon race pace. It should feel like you’re working — steady, strong, and focused — but not on the edge of blowing up.

If you are relatively new to running, the safest way to get started is with walk/run intervals. This will help to minimise the chance of sustaining an injury, and will help to conserve energy so that you can focus on your technique. Start with intervals of 1 min run / 1 min walk and gradually increase the amount of time running while keeping the walking breaks the same. For example:

- Week 1 – 3km Total Distance: Run 1min / Walk 1min

- Week 2 – 3km Total Distance: Run 2min / Walk 1min

- Week 3 – 3km Total Distance: Run 3min / Walk 1min
